passages.title: The Shop That Came to the Door

paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, households in the remote villages of northern England and Scotland did a large part of their shopping without ever leaving home. Twice a week, sometimes more, a converted lorry or van would pull up at the end of the lane, a bell would ring, and residents would climb aboard to buy bread, paraffin, tinned goods and sewing thread. These mobile shops, known locally as 'travellers', filled a gap that fixed retailers could not afford to serve. At their peak in the late 1950s, one trade directory listed more than 2,300 of them operating across Britain. For many families, the arrival of the van was one of the fixed points of the week.

The earliest mobile shops were horse-drawn carts, often run by bakers or grocers who wanted to reach customers beyond walking distance of their premises. The real expansion, however, came after the First World War, when thousands of ex-army lorries were sold off cheaply. Enterprising shopkeepers fitted these vehicles with wooden shelves, a counter at the rear and, in some cases, a small paraffin stove to keep the driver warm in winter. By 1930 a well-equipped van could carry around 400 different items, a range that would have impressed many village shops of the time. Some firms painted their vans in bright colours and gave them names, partly so that customers could recognise them from a distance across open fields.

Running a traveller was demanding work. A typical owner-driver started before dawn, loading stock from a wholesaler in the nearest market town, and might not return until after dark. Routes were planned with great care: each village had to be visited on the same day and at roughly the same time every week, because customers organised their household routines around the van's arrival. Records kept by one Cumbrian operator, Walter Heslop, show that he covered 190 miles a week and served about 340 regular households. His ledgers also reveal that almost a third of his sales were made on credit, with families settling their accounts at the end of each month.

The mobile shop was more than a place to buy goods. For elderly or isolated residents, the weekly visit was frequently their main contact with the outside world. Drivers delivered letters, passed on news from neighbouring farms and occasionally collected prescriptions from the chemist in town. Oral history interviews recorded in the 1990s suggest that many former customers remembered the driver's conversation as clearly as the goods they bought. Some operators even acted as informal bankers, cashing cheques for pensioners who lived many miles from the nearest branch.

From the 1960s onwards, however, the trade entered a long decline. Rising car ownership meant that more rural families could drive to supermarkets, where prices were lower and choice was far greater. At the same time, stricter food hygiene regulations required operators to install refrigeration and running water, investments that many small businesses could not justify. The number of mobile shops fell steadily, and by 1985 fewer than 400 were thought to remain in operation. In some areas the closure of village schools and post offices also reduced the number of people living in remote settlements, shrinking the customer base still further. Operators who survived often did so by specialising, for example in fresh fish or hardware, rather than trying to compete with supermarkets on price.

Recently, though, the idea has begun to return in a new form. Several rural councils have supported community-owned vans that combine a small grocery with services such as parcel collection and library loans. Unlike their predecessors, these vehicles use card readers and online ordering, allowing customers to request specific products in advance. Supporters argue that they reduce the number of individual car journeys and help older residents remain independent. Critics, on the other hand, point out that most of these schemes still depend on public grants and have yet to show that they can survive on sales alone.

Whether the modern traveller will become a permanent feature of rural life remains uncertain. What is clear is that the original mobile shops solved a problem that has never entirely disappeared: how to bring everyday goods to people who live far from the places where those goods are sold. Historians of retailing have begun to take a closer interest in the subject, and a small collection of restored vans can now be seen at a transport museum in County Durham, where visitors are invited to step inside and imagine the busy Saturday rounds of the past.

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the accepted wisdom in language teaching was that the classroom should be a monolingual space. Pupils learning English, French or Spanish were expected to hear and use only the target language, and teachers who slipped into the pupils' home language were often regarded as having failed. The reasoning seemed straightforward: the more exposure learners received to the new language, the faster they would acquire it, and every minute spent in their first language was a minute lost. Textbooks of the period frequently included advice on how to avoid translation altogether, recommending gestures, pictures and demonstrations instead.

Over the past two decades, this assumption has been challenged by a growing body of classroom research. Linguists working in multilingual schools noticed that pupils routinely moved between languages when discussing difficult ideas with one another, even when teachers had banned the practice. Rather than treating this behaviour as a sign of weakness, some researchers began to describe it as a resource. The term 'translanguaging', originally used to describe a bilingual teaching method in Welsh schools, came to refer more broadly to the ways in which multilingual speakers draw on their full range of languages in order to make meaning.

One of the more detailed investigations was carried out over three years in eleven secondary schools in a large port city, where more than forty home languages were spoken. The research team, led by the applied linguist Dr Maren Oduya, compared science lessons in which pupils were permitted to discuss new concepts in any language with lessons conducted strictly in English. Pupils in the flexible classes scored, on average, 12 per cent higher on end-of-unit tests. Perhaps more surprisingly, their written English was no weaker than that of the control group, and in some cases their use of technical vocabulary was more precise.

Oduya's team suggested that the explanation lay in the difference between understanding a concept and expressing it. When pupils first met a complex idea, such as the distinction between mass and weight, they were able to work out its meaning through discussion in the language they knew best. Once the concept was secure, attaching the English terms to it became a relatively simple task. In the English-only lessons, by contrast, many pupils appeared to memorise the vocabulary without fully grasping the idea behind it, and this weakness became evident when they were asked to apply the concept to an unfamiliar problem. Several teachers in the study also reported that pupils who had worked through a concept in their home language asked more questions in the later, English-medium part of the lesson.

Not everyone is persuaded. Critics argue that the benefits reported in such studies may depend heavily on the skill of individual teachers, and that in less carefully managed classrooms the home language can easily come to dominate. There is also a practical difficulty: in a class where pupils speak a dozen different languages, the teacher cannot possibly understand every conversation, and may therefore be unable to identify misunderstandings. A small-scale study in a rural district found that, without clear rules about when each language should be used, pupils' exposure to English fell by almost half within a single term. Some teachers also worry that pupils who share a home language may unintentionally exclude classmates who do not speak it.

Supporters of translanguaging accept that it is not a method that can simply be switched on. They stress that it works best as a planned strategy rather than an informal tolerance of mixed language use. In the classrooms observed by Oduya's team, teachers typically allowed open discussion in any language during the early stages of a task, but required the final written product to be in English. Some schools also produced bilingual glossaries, compiled partly by the pupils themselves, which linked key terms in English to their equivalents in the most widely spoken home languages.

The debate has implications that go beyond language teaching. If pupils' home languages are treated as a tool for learning rather than an obstacle, schools may need to reconsider how they train teachers, design assessments and communicate with parents. For many families, the change of attitude also carries a symbolic value. Parents interviewed during the port city study frequently said that their children had become less reluctant to use the family language at home once it had been welcomed at school, a result that the researchers had not set out to measure but considered among the most significant of the project. Whether such effects can be reproduced in other settings is a question that further research will need to address.

paragraphs.text: When a person asks a company to delete their personal data, the request is, in principle, simple to satisfy: the relevant records are located and erased. For organisations that use machine learning, however, the situation is considerably more complicated. A model trained on millions of examples does not store those examples in a form that can be neatly removed; instead, the information is dispersed across billions of numerical parameters, each shaped slightly by every piece of data the model encountered. Deleting the original record from a database leaves the model's learned behaviour untouched, and in some cases the model may still be able to reproduce fragments of the data it was trained on.

This mismatch has given rise to a field known as machine unlearning, which seeks methods for removing the influence of specific data from a trained model. The most reliable approach is also the most obvious: discard the model and retrain it from scratch without the offending data. For small systems this is practical, but for large models the cost is prohibitive. One estimate, produced by an industry consortium, put the energy required to retrain a single large language model at roughly the annual electricity consumption of 1,200 households, a figure that makes routine retraining in response to individual requests unrealistic.

Researchers have therefore explored cheaper alternatives. One early proposal, sometimes described as 'sharded' training, involves dividing the training data into many separate portions and training a smaller sub-model on each. When a deletion request arrives, only the sub-model that saw the relevant data needs to be retrained. The approach reduces costs substantially, but it has a drawback: models assembled from many independently trained parts tend to perform less well than a single model trained on all the data at once, and the loss of accuracy grows as the number of shards increases. Choosing how many shards to use therefore involves a trade-off between the cost of future deletions and the quality of the model.

A second family of techniques attempts to reverse the effect of particular examples directly, by adjusting the model's parameters in the opposite direction to the changes those examples originally caused. These 'approximate' methods are fast, often requiring only minutes of computation, but they raise a difficult question of verification. Because a model's behaviour emerges from the interaction of vast numbers of parameters, it is hard to demonstrate that the influence of a particular record has genuinely disappeared rather than merely become less visible. In one series of experiments, a team of researchers found that models which appeared to have forgotten certain training examples could be prompted to recall them after a small amount of further training on unrelated material.

The verification problem is not merely technical; it also has legal and ethical dimensions. Data protection laws in several jurisdictions grant individuals a right to have their information erased, but these laws were drafted with conventional databases in mind and say little about statistical models. Regulators have so far been reluctant to state whether an approximately unlearned model satisfies an erasure request. Some legal scholars argue that the law should require only that the model no longer reveals the individual's data; others maintain that any residual influence, however small, amounts to continued processing of personal information. Until the question is settled, companies face considerable uncertainty about what they must do when a request arrives.

There is also a broader concern about who benefits from unlearning. The techniques were initially discussed as a means of protecting privacy, but the same methods could be used to remove material for less admirable reasons: to conceal evidence of biased training data, for instance, or to erase content that a company later finds commercially inconvenient. Because unlearning leaves few visible traces, outsiders may have no way of knowing what has been removed. For this reason, several researchers have proposed that any use of unlearning should be recorded in an independent log, open to inspection by auditors, though no such system yet exists on a large scale.

It seems unlikely that a single solution will emerge. What the debate has already achieved, however, is a shift in how developers think about data at the design stage. Rather than treating training data as a permanent foundation, some organisations now keep detailed records of which data was used to train which model, and structure their systems so that particular sources can be withdrawn later if necessary. In this sense, the ability to forget is gradually becoming part of how machine learning systems are built, rather than a repair attempted after the fact.

passages.title: Echoes in Stone: The Science of Archaeoacoustics

paragraphs.text: Archaeologists have traditionally reconstructed the past through what can be seen and handled: walls, pottery, tools, bones. Sound, by its nature, leaves no direct physical trace, and for most of the discipline's history it was assumed to lie beyond the reach of scientific study. Over the past thirty years, however, a small but increasingly influential group of researchers has argued that the acoustic properties of ancient spaces can be measured, modelled and interpreted, and that doing so may reveal aspects of past experience that conventional methods overlook. The field they have created is known as archaeoacoustics.

The basic techniques are borrowed from architectural acoustics. Researchers place a sound source, typically a loudspeaker emitting a sweeping tone or a sharp burst of noise, at a chosen point within a structure and record the result with microphones positioned elsewhere. From these recordings they calculate measures such as reverberation time, the period taken for a sound to fade by sixty decibels, and identify resonant frequencies at which the space amplifies sound. Where a structure has been partly destroyed, digital models can be used to estimate how it would originally have sounded, although the reliability of such reconstructions depends heavily on assumptions about missing roofs, wall coverings and the number of people present. Measurements are usually repeated several times at each position, and at different times of day, to reduce the influence of wind and background noise.

Some of the most striking results have come from underground chambers. In surveys of a group of Neolithic rock-cut tombs on a Mediterranean island, researchers found that several inner chambers resonated strongly at frequencies between 95 and 120 hertz, a range that falls within the lower register of the adult male voice. Chanting at these frequencies produced a powerful, almost physical sensation that participants described as seeming to come from the walls themselves. Similar resonances have since been reported at sites in Ireland and Peru, prompting speculation that ancient builders may have deliberately shaped spaces to enhance vocal performance.

It is this last claim that has attracted the sharpest criticism. Sceptics point out that almost any enclosed stone chamber of a certain size will resonate within the range of the human voice, simply as a consequence of its dimensions. Demonstrating that a resonance exists is therefore very different from demonstrating that it was intended. In a widely discussed review, the acoustician Tomas Revel argued that many early archaeoacoustic studies had examined only sites where interesting effects were expected, and had rarely compared them with ordinary structures of similar shape. Without such comparisons, he noted, researchers risked mistaking accidental properties for evidence of design. Revel did not reject the field as a whole, however; he argued that its methods needed to become more rigorous if its conclusions were to be taken seriously.

Partly in response to these objections, more recent projects have adopted a comparative approach. A study of prehistoric rock art in a river valley in southern Africa measured echo strength at 64 painted rock shelters and at 58 unpainted shelters nearby. Painted locations were found to produce noticeably stronger echoes on average, a pattern that would be difficult to explain by chance. The researchers were careful, however, not to conclude that the paintings were placed for acoustic reasons alone; they suggested instead that sound may have been one of several factors, alongside visibility and access to water, that made certain locations seem significant.

Archaeoacoustics also raises questions about how evidence of experience should be interpreted. Even if a resonance was deliberately created, we cannot know with confidence how it was perceived. A sensation that a modern visitor finds uncanny may have been ordinary to people who encountered it regularly, and the meanings attached to sound vary enormously between cultures. Written records, where they exist, rarely describe sound in any detail, which makes the task harder still. For this reason, some practitioners have begun to work alongside anthropologists who study present-day communities, not to project modern beliefs onto the past, but to widen the range of possible interpretations that archaeologists consider.

Despite these uncertainties, the field has had a noticeable effect on museum and heritage practice. Several sites now offer visitors recordings or live demonstrations designed to convey how a space would once have sounded, and conservation plans increasingly include acoustic measurements taken before any restoration work begins, since the addition of modern flooring or lighting can subtly alter a chamber's acoustic character. Whether or not the grander claims about intentional design are eventually confirmed, archaeoacoustics has at least ensured that the sensory dimension of ancient places is no longer ignored.

groups.title: Complete the sentences
groups.instruction: Choose NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage for each answer.

questions.text: Reverberation time is the period needed for a sound to fade by sixty ______.
questions.evidence: the period taken for a sound to fade by sixty decibels
questions.explanation: Paragraph B defines reverberation time as the time for a sound **to fade by sixty decibels**.

questions.text: Resonances in the Mediterranean tombs fell within the lower register of the adult male ______.
questions.evidence: within the lower register of the adult male voice
questions.explanation: The frequencies fall within the lower register of the **adult male voice**.

questions.text: Conservation plans now often include acoustic measurements taken before any ______ begins.
questions.evidence: taken before any restoration work begins
questions.explanation: Measurements are taken **before any restoration work begins**, because new flooring or lighting can change a chamber's sound.
